sentences.text: This creature possessed an estimated wingspan of at least 5 meters.
Scientists know it only from an incomplete snout measuring 264 mm in preserved length.
That snout was elongated, transversely compressed, and toothless.
Its name combines the Greek word for air with Titan to allude to the animal's large size.
The preserved snout portion is toothless, features longitudinal striations, and is highly vascularized by numerous small pits.
The remains were found in the Allen Formation of the Neuquén Basin in northern Patagonia.
Aerotitan sudamericanus was named and described in 2012 by Fernando Novas and colleagues.
Fossils were found in Río Negro province, Argentina, in deposits from the Campanian-Maastrichtian of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 million years ago.
It was the first pterosaur of the family Azhdarchidae found in South America.
Within Azhdarchidae, the species is recovered as the sister taxon of Mistralazhdarcho.
A 2025 study placed Aerotitan in a clade with Zhejiangopterus and Mistralazhdarcho within Azhdarchidae, but outside the subfamilies Azhdarchinae and Quetzalcoatlinae.
The animal lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Argentina.
Evidence of fish, turtle fragments, and elasmosaur plesiosaur remains in the sediment suggests it lived in a coastal environment.
It is debated whether Aerotitan belongs to Azhdarchidae or Thalassodromidae, with a 2018 study tentatively placing it in Thalassodromidae but noting the assignment was not well-supported.
